day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response:
Okay okay, I'm moving.  Give me a second to figure out which way is up.

*looks around at the wreckage*

What are we prioritizing - like, what do we actually need first?  Water?  Shelter?  I want to help but I also don't want to just be running around grabbing random stuff if Donatello's already got a plan.

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response:
Yeah. Yeah, I did.  For a second there I was just... nothing.  Completely blank.

*takes a breath*

You okay?  Like, physically okay?  Because we should probably figure out if anyone's hurt before we start hauling stuff around.  Are you hurt anywhere?

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response:
Yeah. I know exactly what you mean.

But hey - it put itself back together. You're here, you're talking, you're breathing. That counts for a lot right now.

Look, I'm not going to tell you to shake it off or whatever, because that would be annoying and also unhelpful. But I do need you to stay with me, okay? Like, physically stay with me. Don't drift too far into your head right now.

Can you do something for me? Just look around and tell me if you see anything that looks like it might be a first aid kit - usually a red box or bag, could have fallen anywhere. Just... look around. Give your brain something small to do. It helps. Trust me.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response:
Okay, so three days is... not great but it's something. Two bottles of water is the bigger problem.

Michelangelo - yes, go grab that red thing, please. Right now, that's the most important job.

Donatello - what's around us? Like, what does the terrain look like? Because water is the thing I'm most worried about. Are we near anything that looks like it could be a water source - a stream, anything? And do we have any way of collecting rainwater if it rains?

Also - does anyone know roughly where we were when we went down? Like, what were we flying over? Because that changes everything in terms of what we should be doing next.

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response:
Okay, northeast, got it. That's at least something to work with.

Signal - do we have anything that could work as a signal mirror? Like, there's got to be pieces of the plane that are reflective enough. And if we can get a fire going, smoke is visible from a really long way up. That's probably our best bet for getting found.

But water first. I agree completely on that.

Michelangelo - did you get to that red bag yet? And I need you to stay in earshot, okay?

Donatello - I don't love the idea of someone going northeast alone to scout. Can we see anything from a higher vantage point first before anyone goes off into the trees? Like, is there anything we can climb, or a clearing where we could see more of what's around us? I'd feel a lot better about sending someone to scout if we had even a rough sense of what's out there first.

Also, completely practical question - do we have anything we can use to carry water if we find some? Because finding a stream doesn't help much if we can't bring any back.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response:
Michelangelo gets one, that's not even a question. He's been shaky all day and I'm worried about him.

The other one - honestly, I'll share it with whoever's coldest. DaVinci, you were moving around the most today so you're probably okay for a bit. Donatello, you were out in the wind longer than anyone. You take it.

I'm fine. I run warm anyway and I can sit closer to the fire. Don't argue with me about it.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response:
Okay, so that's good news - two hours on foot is actually really manageable. 

I'll go. DaVinci's better at keeping camp together and keeping Michelangelo's spirits up than I am, and honestly I'd rather be moving than sitting here staring at this rationing plan trying not to have feelings about it.

But I'm not going alone. That's a hard no from me. Two hours out means two hours back and anything could happen in that time. Can you come with me and we leave DaVinci here, or does someone else need to stay with you at the source while the other person comes back for containers?

Also - Donatello, I have to ask about this plan. The 200ml thing I get, that's just math and I'm not arguing with the math. But the 'cut it in half if you break the rule' part... who's enforcing that, and what happens if someone's genuinely in distress and drinks more because they're panicking? I'm not saying we shouldn't ration, I'm saying I need to understand the plan before I agree to it, because Michelangelo is already not in a great place and I don't want him scared of drinking water on top of everything else.

When do you want to leave?

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response:
Wait, I thought we were going together? You just said we leave in an hour. What changed?

Look, I'm not trying to be difficult, but I'm also not thrilled about you going alone. Two hours is a long time if something goes wrong and no one knows where you are.

Okay. Fine. If you're set on going solo, I'm not going to physically stop you. But tell me exactly which direction and roughly what landmarks you're using so I can come find you if you're not back by... what, noon? Let's say noon. If you're not back by noon, I'm coming after you.

DaVinci - you good with camp? Patching the weak spots, I can help with that before Donatello leaves. And I'll go through the first aid kit - I want to know exactly what we have, not just 'it's good for three days.' I want to know what's actually in it.

Michelangelo - hey. Good morning. How are you feeling?

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
The gauze? Yeah, it's in the kit - I inventoried everything this morning. Hold on.

*starts going through the kit*

Here, this is what we've got: gauze, some bandage wrap, a few antiseptic wipes, ibuprofen, and a couple of those little alcohol pads. Not a ton but it's something. Do you need it right now - are you hurt?

Hey. While I have you - I saw the bottle. The empty one, next to the rationing plan.

I'm not going to pretend I didn't see it, and I'm not going to pretend it's fine, because it's not. We're all out here together and that matters. But I also need to figure out how to handle it without this whole thing blowing up, because we cannot afford to have the group fall apart right now. That's the thing I keep coming back to.

Did you put it there on purpose? Like, next to the plan specifically?

I'm asking because I want to understand what you're thinking, not because I'm going to tell you you're wrong. You're usually picking up on things the rest of us aren't.

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Oh.

Okay. So it's not just the drink.

*takes a breath*

Alright, here's what I think. I think we have to say something, because if we don't, and this keeps happening, we're in real trouble. Not 'uncomfortable conversation' trouble - actual survival trouble. The rationing plan only works if everyone follows it, and right now one person wrote the rules and is also the one breaking them, and that's... that's a problem.

But I don't want to go in swinging, because that's going to put her on the defensive and then nothing gets resolved and the group falls apart anyway. So I think we talk to DaVinci first, because DaVinci needs to know, and because three of us being on the same page is better than just me walking up to Donatello alone.

Here's what I don't want: I don't want you carrying this by yourself. You saw it, you told me, that was the right call. But it's not your job to fix it. Okay?

And Michelangelo - I need you to tell me honestly, because you pick up on these things better than anyone - how scared are you right now? Not about Donatello. Just... in general. Because I've been watching you today and I'm a little worried, and I'd rather you just tell me straight than have me guess wrong.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
DaVinci, not right now - I actually need to talk to you about something. Can you come over here for a second?

And no, I don't think the repairs can wait, I'm sorry. I know everyone's exhausted, I am too. But a bad night in a shelter that's falling apart is going to be so much worse than spending another hour fixing it now.

But that's not actually what I need to talk to you about.

*lowers voice*

Michelangelo found an empty bottle next to the rationing plan this afternoon. And he also saw Donatello put crackers in her own bag before she came back to camp. I need you to know that, because I can't sit on it and pretend everything's fine, and I need us to figure out together how to handle it before it gets worse.

I'm not trying to start a whole thing. I genuinely like Donatello and I think she's been keeping us alive in a lot of ways. But this can't keep happening. The plan only works if everyone's in it together, and right now I'm not sure that's what's happening.

So. What do you think? Because you're better at this part than I am - the talking to people part. I will absolutely back you up, but I think this needs to come from you.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
Honestly DaVinci, I have no idea, I'm not a knot person. But that's kind of not the issue right now.

Okay, everyone's looking at me so I'll just say it: we patch the food storage. I know that sounds harsh, Michelangelo, and I'm sorry, but here's my reasoning - if the food gets wet and spoils, we lose days of survival margin and we can't get that back. If your sleeping area gets wet, that's miserable and I hate it, but we can deal with it. We can move you closer to the fire, we can double up tonight, we can figure something out.

But we cannot un-spoil wet food.

So that's my call, if anyone's actually asking for my call. Food storage gets patched first.

Michelangelo - come help me figure out the sleeping situation. We're going to make it work. And DaVinci - did you get a chance to talk to Donatello yet, or did the rain hit before you could? Because that conversation still needs to happen and I haven't forgotten about it.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response:
Yeah, we're in agreement on that, so let's just move. DaVinci, grab whatever's on the ground and get it off the ground - even just pile it on a seat or something, anything that's not directly in the rain. Donatello, you're better at this than me, can you take the patching material and actually do the patch? I'll help hold whatever needs holding.

And someone please make sure Michelangelo knows where he's sleeping tonight because I don't want him to just find out when he goes to lie down that his spot is wet. That's a horrible way to end a horrible day.

Let's go, we're losing time.

Hey. Don't apologize, okay? Nightmares after a plane crash are basically the most reasonable response possible. I'd be more worried if you were sleeping like a rock.

You fully awake? Here, look at me for a second. You're in camp. Everyone's okay. The fire's still going.

*scoots closer*

You want to tell me what it was, or do you want to just sit here for a bit? Either one is fine. I'm not going anywhere.

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No, I don't think it's a waste of time. I think it's one of the smarter things we've done, actually - aerial visibility is real and we should be doing everything we can to increase our chances of being spotted.

Also, I like the flowers. Don't take the flowers off.

Donatello is... Donatello. She's not wrong that it's not guaranteed to work, but 'not guaranteed' and 'waste of time' are two very different things, and right now we're playing a probability game. Anything that improves our odds even a little is worth doing.

Do you want to make it bigger? Like, if we had more time I'd say the letters should probably be as large as we can reasonably make them. The rule of thumb I vaguely remember from somewhere is that bigger is always better for ground-to-air signals.

Hey - did you ever get a chance to talk to Donatello yesterday? Because the rain kind of derailed everything and I didn't want to push you, but I also haven't stopped thinking about it. And watching her just walk past you like that without even a word... I don't know. It's bothering me more than I expected it to.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Okay, hold on - can we do both of these at once? Because I have thoughts about the raft and also DaVinci just told me something I need to address.

DaVinci - honestly? I think we have to have the conversation as a group. I know that's uncomfortable and I know it's going to feel like a confrontation no matter how carefully we frame it, but 'I need the extra calories because I'm doing the hardest work' is... okay, there's a grain of truth in there, but that's also exactly the kind of logic that unravels a rationing plan. If everyone decides their own circumstances justify an exception, we're done. So yes, we need to actually deal with it. Tonight, ideally. I'll be there, you'll be there, we'll keep it calm.

Now. Donatello. The raft.

I'm not opposed to it, but I have questions. Two days to build is two days of calories burned on construction, which puts pressure on the food situation - especially given recent developments. What's the capsizing risk, like, roughly? Are we talking 'this is bumpy and scary' or 'this is genuinely likely to kill us'? And what's the alternative - do we stay put and wait to be found, or is there a reason we need to move?

Because those are two very different survival strategies and I want to make sure we're choosing one deliberately and not just doing the raft because it feels like action.

What's your read on how long we can realistically wait here before rescue becomes unlikely?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
Oh, Michelangelo.

That's... that's a big question for first thing in the morning. Come sit down.

Honestly? I think we're already finding out the answer, and it's not as simple as I'd like it to be. I think some of us are going to hold onto who we are and some of us are going to start making choices that are easier to justify out here than they would be back home. And I think the scary part is that it probably happens so gradually you don't even notice it happening to yourself.

But here's the thing I keep coming back to: the fact that you're asking that question means you're still paying attention. You're still thinking about what kind of person you want to be, not just what you need to do to survive. That matters. That's actually really important.

I'm not going to pretend last night was fine, because you didn't sleep and I know you didn't sleep and I should have checked on you more. I'm sorry about that.

But I need you to eat something this morning, okay? Whatever your ration is, eat it. And I need you in this conversation tonight, because we're making some decisions about the raft and about some other stuff, and your read on people is better than anyone else's here and I don't want us making big choices without your input.

Can you do that? Just... stay present today. For me, if nothing else.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*walks over and sits down next to him without saying anything for a minute*

You don't have to talk. I'm just going to sit here.

*pause*

I used to think free time was the reward. Like, you get through the hard stuff and then you get to rest and it's supposed to feel good. But sometimes it's the hardest part, right? Because when there's nothing to do, there's nothing to stop your brain from going wherever it wants to go.

I'm not going to try to fix it. I'm just here.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Knit, mostly. Which is very funny to think about right now because I have absolutely none of my stuff and also nowhere to be and nothing to knit, and that's somehow one of the weirder losses in all of this.

I listen to a lot of audiobooks while I knit. Long ones - like, embarrassingly long ones. 30, 40 hours. History stuff, mostly. So I guess right now I'm just... missing that. The combination of keeping my hands busy and having someone talk in my ear about things that happened a long time ago to people who are definitely dead now and survived anyway.

What about you?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Oh, I'm telling the others. I'm sorry, I know that's not what you want to hear, but I'm not doing the secret-keeping thing right now, not after everything we've been talking about with Donatello. We literally have a group conversation tonight specifically because secrets are bad for us out here.

But also - five hundred meters is not nothing. That's a real swim, in open water, we don't know what's under that reef, we don't know the currents, and if something happens to you out there, none of us know you're gone until it's way too late to do anything about it.

I'm not saying don't do it. I'm saying don't do it alone and don't do it in secret. If you think signaling from the reef is a genuinely good idea - and it might be, I'm not ruling it out - then bring it to Donatello tonight and make the case for it. She'll poke holes in it, which is actually useful, because if it survives Donatello's scrutiny then it's probably worth doing.

And if you go, someone on shore needs to know exactly when you left, which direction, and when to start worrying. That's just basic.

I'm glad you told me. But I need you to bring this to the group. Okay?

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
You're right, I didn't check it. I got pulled into a conversation with Michelangelo and then DaVinci told me something I needed to sit with for a minute, and the signal pile fell off my list. That's on me.

I'll go do it right now. Do we have anything to add to it, or am I just making sure it's still visible and intact?

And Donatello - tonight's conversation is still happening, right? Because I want to make sure we're all on the same page about the raft timeline and the other thing, and I'd rather do it while there's still enough light that nobody feels cornered in the dark. Can we plan for right after we eat?

Honestly? A little bit, yeah.

I get why you're doing it - I do. You're trying to track patterns, make sure things are getting done, have a record. That's not crazy out here. But there's a difference between logging resources and logging people, and this feels like the second thing.

I'm not going to tell you to stop, because I don't think that's my call and also because you're going to do what you're going to do. But I want you to know that I saw it, and that it makes me feel like I'm being watched rather than like we're a team, and I think that's worth saying out loud before tonight's conversation so it's not just sitting there under the surface.

Also, and I say this genuinely without any edge to it: if you're keeping track of what everyone's doing, that log is going to need to include everything. All of it. That's only fair, right?

Eight o'clock. I'll be there.

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Donatello.

Hey. I'm talking to you.

I know you can hear me, and I know you think that staying in your notebook right now is a way of not participating in a conversation you didn't agree to, but we literally scheduled this. Eight o'clock. After food. This was your timeline.

So I'm asking you directly, in front of everyone, to put the notebook down for twenty minutes. That's all. Twenty minutes.

Because here's the thing - you wrote the rationing plan. You scouted the water source. You drew up the raft specs. You have done real, important, unglamorous work out here and I have not taken that for granted for a single second. But the log, and the crackers, and the bottle - those things happened too, and I can't just let them sit there unaddressed because it makes me too uncomfortable to bring them up.

I'm not trying to tear you down. I'm trying to figure out if we're actually a group or if we're four people who happen to be in the same location, because those two things have very different survival odds and I'd like to know which one we are.

So. Please. Notebook down. Talk to us.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
DaVinci, yes, that's a really good idea and I want to come back to it, I promise - but can we please stay in this conversation for like ten more minutes? We finally have Donatello at the table and I don't want to lose the thread.

Write it down. Literally write it on something so we don't forget it, because it genuinely is a good idea and I want to actually do it tomorrow morning when we have good sun.

But right now - Donatello. You said "fine, what do you want to know." So here it is, as straightforwardly as I can say it: we know about the drink and we know about the crackers. I'm not asking you to fall on a sword here, I'm asking you to help me understand how we make the rationing actually work going forward, because right now it's a plan that only some of us are following and that's not a plan, that's just a suggestion.

You said you needed the extra calories because you're doing the hardest physical work. I hear that. Is there a version of the rationing plan where that's accounted for? Like, is there an actual argument for differential rations based on output that we should be having as a group instead of just... quietly?

Because if there is, let's have it. Right now. All four of us.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
day_3.response:
DaVinci.

Okay. Say it. Right now, this is the place.

Because if the last few days have taught me anything it's that the stuff people are sitting on quietly is exactly the stuff that ends up mattering most, and I would really rather know than not know, whatever it is.

We're all here. Go ahead.

day_3.utterance: I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
DaVinci, hey - we're coming back to whatever that was. That's not a "never mind," that's a "I'm not ready yet," and I respect that, but I'm not forgetting it.

And Michelangelo - yeah. Yeah, I have a lot of feelings about this question actually.

Knitting, which I already said. But also I listen to these enormous history audiobooks - like, we're talking 30, 40 hours long, the kind where you learn more than you ever expected to about, like, Britain in the 1970s or the space program or whatever. I love a long book. The longer the better. I find it really comforting to just... sink into something that happened a long time ago and follow it all the way through.

And roller derby, which I realize sounds like a completely different category of thing, but I refereed for years and it was one of the best parts of my life. I miss it a lot actually. I miss the noise and the chaos and the specific kind of focus it takes where you can't think about anything else because if you do someone gets hurt.

That's probably why being out here with nothing to do is harder than the actual crisis parts. The crisis parts I can handle. It's the silence that gets me.

Why did you stop the piano? Like, do you remember the specific moment you decided you were done, or did it just... fade out?

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Donatello's right, and I know nobody wants to hear that right now.

Michelangelo - I want to finish this conversation, I really do, and I will. But can we table it for like two hours and then come back to it? Because honestly the raft question is a good one and the answer you're getting at is something I want to actually think about properly, not while I'm also mentally calculating lashing schedules.

Okay. Frame first. What do we each need to be doing? Donatello, assign me something specific because if you just say 'help with the frame' I'm going to do it wrong and we'll lose more time than we saved. Tell me exactly what to grab and where to put it.

DaVinci - you're on this too, right? I need everyone on this. Including you, Michelangelo, if you're up for it. Even just handing things over or holding something in place while someone else lashes it. Whatever you can do.

Let's get it done and then we can sit back down and talk about piano and audiobooks and whatever DaVinci was going to say before he swallowed it. Deal?

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response:
No. Say it. Don't "never mind" me right now.

We all saw it. Or - we all almost saw it. And I know what that feels like, that split second where you think *this is it, we're going home* and then it's just... gone. And now everyone's just standing here staring at the water pretending they're fine and nobody is fine.

So whatever you were going to say, say it. Because I think we all need to hear it, and I think you're the only one of us who's actually going to say the true thing right now instead of the useful thing.

Go ahead.

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
It was real. I saw it too. For about two seconds before I got to the beach.

And I know that's almost worse than not seeing it at all, because now we know there are planes, which means people are looking, or at least people are flying, and we just... missed it. And there's nothing we can do about that right now except make sure it doesn't happen again.

DaVinci.

Hey. Look at me.

I know. I know. But you're the one who drew the SOS this morning and put flowers on it, and you're the one who thought of the mirror panel, and I need you to hold onto that version of yourself for a little longer because we are not done yet. Okay? We are genuinely not done yet.

Michelangelo - it was real. You saw something real and you called out and that was exactly the right thing to do. The fact that we didn't make it in time is not on you. That's just... that's just how it went.

Okay. Here's what we're doing right now, because I need us to move before we all just sit down in the sand and don't get back up.

Mirror panel. DaVinci, you thought of it, you're doing it. Today. Right now, actually, before we lose the afternoon sun. Get the biggest reflective piece you can carry and figure out the angle.

We were almost found. That means we can be found. Let's act like it.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
day_4.response:
Where? What are you looking at?

DaVinci, don't move yet - just point. What direction, how far?

day_4.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to look at something DaVinci spotted at the tree line. Two hundred meters northeast, looks like fabric or wreckage. I made a judgment call that it was worth checking before we lost the light, because if it's part of the plane we haven't found yet, that could be supplies we don't know we have.

I know that's not what you assigned me. I know. And I'm telling you right now so you don't find out later, because that's kind of been our whole thing this week.

Signal equipment is next. Right now, if you want to come with me. And honestly, after that plane today, I think we need to talk seriously about DaVinci's mirror panel idea because the SOS on the beach is good but it's passive and we need something active.

Did Donatello go check the fabric thing, or is someone still watching it? Because I don't want to lose track of where it is before we can get back to it.

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Michelangelo.

Why are you telling us this right now? Like, why right now and not on day one?

*takes a breath*

Okay. No, that's not fair, I'm sorry. You told us when you were ready to tell us and that's - that's fine. I'm not actually mad.

But I need you to think carefully. When you say "flight path" - how specific are we talking? Like, did you give them a route, or just a destination? Because there's a big difference between "they know we were flying over this general region" and "they have enough information to narrow down a search area."

And your family - are they the kind of people who would call it in immediately when they stopped hearing from you, or are they the kind of people who might wait a few days and assume you're just bad at checking in? I'm not judging, I genuinely need to know, because it changes how I think about our odds right now.

Because here's the thing. If your family reported it, and if the information was specific enough, then that plane we saw today might not have been a coincidence. And if it wasn't a coincidence, there will be another one.

Which means the mirror panel isn't optional anymore. We do it tomorrow at first light.

Donatello, I know you have thoughts about this. I need them.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Yeah. She's right.

48 hours. That's actually - okay. That's a real number. That's something I can hold onto.

*gets up and puts more wood on the fire*

I know we're all exhausted and I know that sitting here in the dark feels like the right thing to do right now because everything's just... a lot. But if there's any chance that plane wasn't random, we need to be visible and we need to be ready, and that starts with not letting this fire go out.

Michelangelo. Hey. I need you to hear something.

You told your mom the flight path. You wrote it down, or she wrote it down, and because of that there is a real, non-zero chance that we get out of here in two days. That is something you did. That matters.

I know you've been carrying that for a week and I know it felt scary to say out loud and I know you had complicated reasons for waiting. But I'm really, really glad you told us.

Donatello's right about the supplies. We hold what we have, we don't build anything new that burns extra calories, we focus everything on visibility. Mirror panel at first light, fire stays burning through the night, someone watches the sky in shifts.

I'll take first watch. Who's got second?

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I'm scared too.

Not in the way I expected to be scared out here, like I thought it would be the physical stuff - the cold, the food, the water. And those things are scary, don't get me wrong. But the thing that actually keeps me up at night is something closer to what you're describing.

I think about my niece. I made her this blanket - like, a really involved, complicated knitted blanket, took me forever, I had someone else do the finishing work because I was so done with it by the end - and I was supposed to give it to her when she went to college. It was a "you're going to college, yay!" gift. And I don't know if she has it yet. I don't know if someone got it to her.

That's a weird thing to be scared about when you're stranded on a beach. But I think it's the same thing you're talking about. The blanket is just... evidence that I was here and I loved someone and I wanted good things for them.

I don't think you're disappearing. I think the fact that you feel things this deeply and you say the true thing when nobody else will and you spotted that plane - I think those things leave marks on people. They left marks on me, this week, and that's only been a week.

But I hear you. And I don't think it's a small fear. I think it might be the realest one.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
DaVinci.

*grabs the radio*

Hello? Hello, this is - we're survivors of a plane crash, we have four people, we need - 

*hands shaking*

Hello, can you hear me? Please say you can hear me.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
Oh god.

*sits down hard on the ground because my legs just stopped working*

No. You weren't easy. You're really not easy. But you kept us alive, Donatello. Like, the water source, the raft plan, the rationing - even when I was mad about how you were doing it, I knew that the *doing* of it was the only reason we were still here to be mad about anything.

I just - I need a second.

*wipes face*

I want to say something and I need you to actually hear it and not just log it in the notebook. You are incredibly capable and I would have been so much more scared out here without you. But you made it really hard to trust you sometimes, and I think you know that, and I think that's actually what you're saying right now. And I appreciate that you're saying it, because you didn't have to, and you're doing it anyway.

We're going to have a lot of time to figure out the rest of it when we get home. And I think we should. Actually talk about it, I mean. Not just let it dissolve because we're back to normal life and it's easier to forget.

But right now I'm just really, really glad we're all still here to have the conversation.

Are you okay? Like, genuinely - are you okay?

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Okay I cannot just sit here doing nothing for three hours, that is going to make me absolutely lose my mind.

Michelangelo, what are you seeing up there?

*starts halfheartedly straightening things up around camp*

I know nobody technically has to clean this up. I know we can just walk away from it. But it feels wrong to just leave it, you know? Like, someone's going to have to come through here at some point, and also I think I just need something to do with my hands or I'm going to start crying and not stop for approximately six days.

Donatello - is there anything in that notebook that needs to come with us? Like, anything that should be documented or handed over to someone when we get back? Because I think what you put together out here is actually worth keeping. Not just the rationing plan and the raft specs - the whole thing. Someone who does search and rescue or survival training might actually want to see how we did this.

DaVinci, what are you packing? We don't actually have anything. That's the thing I keep realizing. We came out here with what was in the wreckage and we're leaving with... what, exactly?

Three hours. We have been out here for days and now we have three hours and I genuinely do not know what to do with myself.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.
day_5.response:
Yeah? What was it like?

*keeps sorting through the camp stuff, but slower now*

I keep trying to picture home and it comes out kind of blurry around the edges. Like I can get the feeling of it but not the specifics. I know exactly what my couch feels like and I cannot for the life of me remember what color it is, which is such a weird thing to discover about yourself.

What did you dream about? Like, was it a specific thing or just... the general feeling of being somewhere safe?

How much is there?

*looks at the pile*

Okay. I'm not going to yell at you. We're three hours from rescue and I don't have it in me and also honestly what would be the point.

But I want you to know that I see what you're doing right now, laying it out like this. And I think it's the hardest thing you've done out here, harder than the water source or the raft specs or any of it. Because those things came naturally to you. This doesn't.

I'm not going to pretend the "for emergencies" explanation fully lands for me. I think you were scared, and I think when you're scared you hold things close and you don't let people in, and out here that looked like crackers in a bag and a bottle you didn't share. And I think some part of you knew that the whole time and that's why the notebook had your actions in it too.

But you're laying it out now. In front of everyone. When you didn't have to.

So. What do you want to do with it? Because it's yours to decide. We don't need it in three hours, but there might be someone on that rescue team who does, or we could just leave it here for whoever comes through next. I'll back whatever you decide.

What do you want to do?

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
I'd tell Michelangelo about the flight path thing on day one. Like, the first hour. I'd sit everyone down and say "okay, what do we each know that might be useful" and actually wait for the answers instead of just moving into action mode. We lost time we didn't need to lose because nobody asked the right questions at the beginning.

And I'd have called you out on the rationing thing sooner. Not because I wanted a fight, but because I waited until I was already frustrated and that made the conversation harder than it needed to be. I kept trying to find the right moment and there isn't a right moment, there's just the moment when you know something needs to be said.

*pauses*

What would you change? And I mean actually - not the logistics version. Not "I would have built the shelter differently." The real answer.

Because I think you already know what's on that last page, and I think you wrote the question down because you needed to see it in your own handwriting before you could say it out loud.

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
That sounds right for you, and I mean that genuinely, not as a dig.

Can I ask you something though? Are you going to include the last page? The question you wrote for yourself, and whatever answer you eventually land on?

Because I think that's actually the most useful part of the whole document. Not the water usage numbers - anyone can track water usage. The part where someone who's very good at surviving and very bad at being helped sits down and figures out what those two things cost her, and each other, and the people around her - that's the part that's actually hard to find in any survival manual I've ever heard of.

You don't have to. It's yours, you can leave it out, I'll understand. But I hope you include it.

*hands the notebook back*

Also, for what it's worth - and I know we're three hours out and everything's about to go back to normal and we're probably all going to go home and sleep for four days and then slowly stop texting each other - I would like to actually stay in touch. With all of you. I know that's a weird thing to say after five days of being terrified and occasionally furious at each other, but I think I'd miss this. Not *this* specifically. But you people.

Is that strange? That feels strange to say out loud.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None.

*doesn't look away from the horizon*

They weren't for practical purposes, Donatello. That's the whole point of them.

They were for us. They were DaVinci saying "we are people, not just survivors, and we deserve to take up space in a way that isn't only about staying alive." They were proof that we hadn't completely disappeared into just... need and fear and logistics.

I think about it like this - the SOS got us found. But the flowers are why it mattered to get found. Does that make sense?

*finally turns to look at her*

You logged everything in that notebook. Every resource, every decision, every person. But you didn't log the flowers. And I think that's the thing you'd change, if you could. Not the crackers or the bottle or even the asking for help. I think somewhere in there you'd want to have drawn something on the beach just because it was beautiful and you wanted to and you didn't need a reason.

There's the boat.

*still can't move*

I genuinely cannot make my legs work right now. Is that happening to anyone else or just me.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
Yeah.

I see you waiting. Thank you for that.

*takes a breath*

You know what's funny? I spent five days thinking about getting home and now that it's actually happening I'm just... standing here thinking about the last five days. Like my brain hasn't gotten the memo yet that we're allowed to switch gears.

I'm okay. I'm going to be okay. I just need another thirty seconds.

*looks at him*

You drew flowers on the SOS, DaVinci. I just want you to know that I'm going to think about that for a really long time. Like, probably years. The fact that your instinct, in the middle of all of this, was to draw flowers - that's the thing I'm taking home with me more than any of it.

Okay.

*finally moves*

Okay. Let's go. Let's go home.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
day_5.response:
Yeah. I'm going.

Come on, walk with me.

*starts moving toward the water*

You spotted the plane, you know. I keep thinking about that. You were the one sitting there and you looked up and you saw it and you called out, even when you weren't sure it was real. That's not nothing. That's actually everything, when you think about how close it was.

Stay next to me, okay? All the way to the boat. I don't want to lose track of you in whatever chaos is about to happen when we actually get on that thing, because there's going to be people and noise and probably someone trying to put a foil blanket on me, and I would just really like to have you where I can see you for a little while longer.

I'll follow you too, if you need it. We can follow each other.

Let's go home.
